facts.text: Berhtwald was elected Archbishop of Canterbury.
Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos were burnt at the stake in Brussels, becoming the first Lutherans executed by the Council of Brabant.

links.title: Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos

facts.text: The Westminster Assembly of Divines first assembled to restructure the Church of England.
Williamite forces defeated the Jacobites at the Battle of the Boyne near Drogheda, marking a turning point in the Williamite War in Ireland.
Thomas Lempriere and James Clark Ross carved a sandstone marker on Tasmania's Isle of the Dead, one of the oldest benchmarks for measuring sea level rise.
Belgium introduced its first series of postage stamps, known as epaulettes.

American Civil War: Confederate general Robert E. Lee launched a series of disjointed and ultimately unsuccessful assaults on the nearly impregnable Union position on Malvern Hill in Henrico County, Virginia.
The Remington No. 1, the first commercially successful typewriter, went on sale.

First World War: The first day of the Battle of Albert, the opening phase of the Battle of the Somme, became the bloodiest day in the British Army 's history, with 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 deaths.
Seven of the sixteen American railroad labor organizations staged a nationwide strike that lasted two months.
The Singapore Improvement Trust was founded to oversee the construction of public housing in Singapore, where more than three quarters of residents live.
The first flight departed New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport, then known as New York International Airport.
B. Anthony Stewart is credited with the first image on the cover of National Geographic featuring the 49-star flag of the United States after Alaska 's admission to the Union as a U.S. state.

links.title: List of National Geographic cover stories (1959 and 1960s)

facts.text: Sony introduced the Walkman, a portable audio player that changed listening habits by offering users the ability to play one's own choice of music.
A North Korean Ilyushin Il-62M jet crashed into the Fouta Djallon mountains in Guinea, killing all 23 people on board.
Legislative powers in Scotland were first devolved from the Scottish Office in London to the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh.
Bashkirian Airlines Flight 2937 and DHL Flight 611 collided in mid-air over Überlingen, Germany, killing all 71 people aboard both aircraft.
Rioting erupted in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, over allegations of fraud surrounding the recent legislative election.
American Revolutionary War: Five American privateer vessels raided the British settlement at Lunenburg, Nova Scotia (depicted).
The first Grant Park Music Festival was held in Chicago's Grant Park.
Second World War: The Grand Quartier Général of the French Army was disbanded, following the French surrender.
Ghana became a republic, with Kwame Nkrumah as its first president.
The Belfast Banking Company, which issued banknotes in Northern Ireland, merged with its rival Northern Bank.
Li Shimin led his forces to assassinate his rival brothers in a coup for the imperial throne of Tang China.
The bodies of Emperor Gaozong of Tang and Empress Wu Zetian were interred in the Qianling Mausoleum.
First English Civil War: The combined forces of Scottish Covenanters and English Parliamentarians defeated Royalist troops at the Battle of Marston Moor.
On the Feast of the Visitation, Bach led the first performance of his Meine Seel erhebt den Herren, BWV 10, based on the German Magnificat.

links.title: Meine Seel erhebt den Herren, BWV 10

facts.text: The French frigate Méduse ran aground off the coast of present-day Mauritania, with the survivors escaping on a makeshift raft, depicted in Théodore Géricault 's painting The Raft of the Medusa.
U.S. president James A. Garfield was fatally shot by Charles J. Guiteau at the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad station in Washington, D.C.
A German SS unit arrived in Vilnius, Lithuania, and began the systematic execution of up to 100,000 people over the next three years.
The Civil Rights Act was signed into law, outlawing segregation in schools, at the workplace, and other facilities that served the general public in the United States.

links.title: Racial segregation in the United States

facts.text: More than a year after the end of the Vietnam War, North and South Vietnam officially merged under communist rule to form the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
Israeli–Palestinian conflict: An Arab man rammed a loader into traffic in Jerusalem, killing three people and injuring 40 others.
The International Astronomical Union announced that the fourth and fifth moons of Pluto to be discovered would be named Kerberos and Styx, respectively.
American Revolutionary War: French troops landed near St. George's, Grenada, and began their capture of the island.
Singing Revolution: The Soviet economic blockade of Lithuania was lifted when the Lithuanian parliament agreed to suspend the effects of their act to re-establish Lithuania as a state.

image.caption: Date 18 April – 2 July 1990 (78 days) Location Lithuania Result Blockade lifted Negotiations over the future of Lithuanian-USSR relations started Effects of the Act of the Re-Establishment of the State of Lithuania suspended Statehood de facto preserved Expiration of the suspension leads to January Events Soviet aggression on Lithuania's borders

links.title: Act of the Re-Establishment of the State of Lithuania

facts.text: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets by J. K. Rowling, the second novel of the Harry Potter series, was published.

links.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets

facts.text: In the Indonesian province of Aceh on the northern end of Sumatra, a M w 6.1 strike-slip earthquake killed at least 35 people and injured 276 others.
A landslide at a jade mine in Hpakant killed 175–200 miners, the deadliest mining accident in Burmese history.
Civil wars of the Tetrarchy: Roman emperor Constantine the Great defeated his former colleague Licinius at the Battle of Adrianople.
French and Indian War: George Washington surrendered Fort Necessity in Pennsylvania, the only military surrender in his career.
American Revolutionary War: Loyalists and Iroquois killed over 300 Patriots at the Battle of Wyoming in Pennsylvania.
Confederate forces were defeated by the Union Army on the last day of the Battle of Gettysburg, a turning point in the American Civil War.

image.caption: Date July 1–3, 1863 Location Gettysburg, Pennsylvania , U.S. 39°48′41″N 77°13′33″W ﻿ / ﻿ 39.81139°N 77.22583°W ﻿ / 39.81139; -77.22583 Result Union victory [ 1 ]

facts.text: On the 75th anniversary of the end of the Battle of Gettysburg, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the Eternal Light Peace Memorial.
SS United States departed New York Harbor on her maiden voyage, on which completion she became the fastest ocean liner to cross the Atlantic.
Second World War: The Royal Navy attacked the French fleet at Mers El Kébir, fearing that the ships would fall into Axis hands after the French–German armistice.

image.caption: Date 3 July 1940 Location Off Mers El Kébir , French Algeria , North Africa 35°43′10″N 0°41′20″W ﻿ / ﻿ 35.71944°N 0.68889°W ﻿ / 35.71944; -0.68889 Result See Aftermath

facts.text: Dan-Air Flight 1903 crashed into the slopes of the Montseny Massif in Catalonia, Spain, killing all 112 people aboard.
British singer David Bowie retired his stage persona Ziggy Stardust in a surprise announcement on the last day of a 17-month tour.
US president Jimmy Carter signed a presidential finding, authorizing covert operations to aid the mujahideen against the Soviet-backed Democratic Republic of Afghanistan.
General Abdel Fattah el-Sisi led a coalition to depose President Mohamed Morsi in a coup d'état in Cairo, suspending the Egyptian Constitution of 2012.
Mauritius campaign of 1809–1811: A French frigate squadron under Guy-Victor Duperré defeated a convoy of three British East Indiamen near the Comoro Islands.
The Troubles: The British Army began the Falls Curfew in Belfast, Northern Ireland, which resulted in greater Irish republican resistance.
The US Navy warship Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Persian Gulf, killing all 290 people aboard.
Same-sex marriage became legal in Spain with the coming into effect of a law passed by the Cortes Generales.
In Arizona, the Boundary Fire burned out after 32 days, burning 17,788 acres (7,199 ha) of the Coconino and Kaibab National Forests.
Chinese astronomers recorded the sudden appearance of a " guest star ", later identified as the supernova that created the Crab Nebula.

First English Civil War: Royalist forces defeated the Parliamentarians at the Battle of Burton Bridge, securing a crossing of the River Trent for a convoy of supplies travelling with Queen Henrietta Maria.
The Grand Junction Railway, the world's first long-distance railway with steam traction, opened between Birmingham and Newton Junction.
In a boat on the River Thames from Oxford to Godstow, author Lewis Carroll told Alice Liddell and her sisters a story that later formed the basis for his book Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
American Civil War: Confederate forces failed in an attempt to recapture the Union -occupied Helena, Arkansas.
World War I: Allied forces led by the Australian general John Monash won the Battle of Hamel, demonstrating the effectiveness of combined-arms techniques in trench warfare.
The Holocaust: During the German occupation of Latvia, a number of synagogues in Riga were set on fire, killing many Jews who were confined within.

links.title: German occupation of Latvia during World War II

facts.text: German AB-Aktion in Poland: After capturing Lwów, the Nazis executed professors of the University of Lwów along with their families.
The aircraft carrying Władysław Sikorski, prime minister of the Polish government-in-exile, crashed off Gibraltar, killing him and fifteen others and leading to several conspiracy theories.
The Brazilian cruiser Bahia was accidentally sunk by one of its own crewmen, killing more than 300 people.
William Shockley announced the invention of the junction transistor, for which he, John Bardeen, and Walter Houser Brattain later won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Israeli forces raided Uganda's Entebbe International Airport to free hostages taken by hijackers on Air France Flight 139.
Four Iranian diplomats were kidnapped after they were stopped at a checkpoint in northern Lebanon by Lebanese Phalange forces; their fates remain unknown.
The monster movie Pulgasari, the most-widely-seen North Korean film ever made, premiered in Tokyo, Japan.
Byzantine emperor Theodosius II proclaimed his elder sister Aelia Pulcheria as Augusta.
In Philadelphia, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, announcing that the thirteen American colonies were no longer a part of the British Empire.
In what is known as " The Miracle of Bern ", West Germany defeated Hungary 3–2 to win the FIFA World Cup.
Kylie Minogue 's first album, Kylie, was released, and went on to top the charts in the UK and New Zealand.
Keir Starmer leads the Labour Party to a landslide victory in the United Kingdom general election, ending fourteen years of Conservative rule.
Thomas Cook, the founder of the British travel company Thomas Cook & Son, organised his first excursion, escorting about 500 people from Leicester to Loughborough.
Second World War: Canadian troops defeated the last German counterattacks against Carpiquet, Normandy, France.
Named after Bikini Atoll, the site of the nuclear-weapons test Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, the modern bikini was introduced at a fashion show in Paris.
Elvis Presley recorded his first single, " That's All Right ", at Sun Records in Memphis, Tennessee.
Two days after the death of their founder Brian Jones, the Rolling Stones performed at a free festival in Hyde Park, London, in front of more than a quarter of a million fans.
Juvénal Habyarimana orchestrated a bloodless coup d'état of the Rwandan government and began a totalitarian dictatorship.

image.caption: Date 5 July 1973 Location Kigali , Rwanda Result Coup successful

facts.text: United States National Security Council member Oliver North was given a suspended sentence, probation, and community service for his part in the Iran–Contra affair.
Indonesia held its first direct presidential elections, which resulted in the election of Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono as President of Indonesia after the second round on September 20.
The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting hours after North Korea reportedly tested at least seven ballistic missiles.
A series of violent riots broke out in Ürümqi, the capital city of Xinjiang in China.
The Staffordshire Hoard, the largest collection of Anglo-Saxon gold ever discovered, consisting of more than 1,500 items, was found near Hammerwich in Staffordshire.
The Shard in London was inaugurated as the tallest building in Europe, with a height of 310 m (1,020 ft), but was surpassed by Moscow's Mercury City Tower four months later.

links.title: List of tallest buildings in Europe

facts.text: Algiers surrendered to French invaders, ending the Regency of Algiers.

image.caption: Motto: دار الجهاد Bulwark of the Holy War [ 3 ] [ 4 ]

facts.text: Brazilian Army rebels took over Fort Copacabana and launched a rebellion in Rio de Janeiro against President Epitácio Pessoa and President-elect Artur Bernardes.
The Hormel Foods Corporation introduced Spam, the canned precooked meat product that would eventually enter into pop culture, folklore, and urban legend.
Korean War: In the first encounter between North Korean and American forces, an unprepared and undisciplined U.S. Army task force was routed at the Battle of Osan.
An explosion at a petrochemical plant in Channelview, Texas, killed 17 people and injured five others.
The Ottoman Empire made a final attempt to conquer the island of Malta, but were repulsed by the Knights Hospitaller.
Troops loyal to James II of England defeated those of James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth at the Battle of Sedgemoor, the final battle of the Monmouth Rebellion.
American Revolutionary War: American troops at Fort Ticonderoga in New York completed a retreat from advancing British forces, causing an uproar among the American public.
Napoleon 's French forces defeated Archduke Charles' Austrian army at the Battle of Wagram, the decisive confrontation of the War of the Fifth Coalition.
First World War: The British and French prime ministers, H. H. Asquith and René Viviani, met at Calais to discuss future offensives including the Gallipoli campaign.
First World War: Russian troops won a victory in the Battle of Kostiuchnówka, with the Polish Legions playing a key role on the Austro-Hungarian side.

links.title: Polish Legions in World War I

facts.text: A major breach of the Manchester Bolton & Bury Canal in England sent millions of gallons of water cascading 300 feet (90 m) into the River Irwell.
The Story Bridge in Brisbane, the longest cantilever bridge in Australia, was opened by Sir Leslie Wilson, Governor of Queensland.

links.title: List of longest cantilever bridge spans

facts.text: Second World War: After a three-month siege, the Italian garrison of Saïo (in modern-day Ethiopia) surrendered to Belgian, British and Ethiopian troops.
The Troubles: In response to the Drumcree conflict, five days of unrest began in nationalist districts of Northern Ireland.
Jadranka Kosor became the first female prime minister of Croatia.
Gunmen attacked a secondary school in Mamudo, Yobe State, Nigeria, killing 42 people, mostly students.
In the first fatal accident involving a Boeing 777 airliner, Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crashed on final approach to San Francisco International Airport, resulting in three deaths.
The last monarch of the House of York and the Plantagenet dynasty, Richard III, was crowned King of England.
French Revolutionary Wars: A Royal Navy squadron failed to eliminate a smaller French Navy squadron at Algeciras before they could join their Spanish allies.
The United States conducted the Sedan nuclear test as part of Project Plowshare, a program to investigate the use of nuclear explosions for civilian purposes.
After visiting several Asian communist countries, Romanian leader Nicolae Ceaușescu gave a speech on a number of neo-Stalinist and socialist-realist ideals, which became known as the July Theses.
A Palestinian Islamic Jihad member carried out a suicide attack by hijacking a bus and forcing it into a ravine near Kiryat Ye'arim, Israel.
Joan of Arc was declared innocent of heresy in a retrial twenty-five years after her death.

links.title: Rehabilitation trial of Joan of Arc

facts.text: Anglo-Scottish Wars: A dispute between Sir John Forster and Sir John Carmichael led to a Scottish raid on Northumberland, England, in which 27 men were killed.
Outraged by the XYZ Affair, the United States rescinded its treaties with France, resulting in the undeclared Quasi-War, fought entirely at sea.
War of the Second Coalition: The British Royal Navy force attacked the well-defended French anchorage of Dunkirk (depicted), capturing a French frigate.
Inspired by the Folies Bergère of Paris, American impresario Florenz Ziegfeld Jr. staged the first of his Ziegfeld Follies.

image.caption: Born Florenz Edward Ziegfeld Jr. ( 1867-03-21 ) March 21, 1867 Chicago, Illinois U.S.

facts.text: The Peel Commission published a report stating that the League of Nations ' Mandate for Palestine had become unworkable and recommended the partition of British-administered Mandatory Palestine into two states.

The secret police of Ngô Đình Nhu, brother and chief political adviser of South Vietnamese president Ngô Đình Diệm, attacked a group of American journalists who were covering a protest during the Buddhist crisis.
After writing a letter to Soviet premier Yuri Andropov, American schoolgirl Samantha Smith visited the Soviet Union as Andropov's personal guest, becoming known as "America's Youngest Ambassador".
Yugoslav Wars: The signing of the Brioni Agreement ended the Ten-Day War between SFR Yugoslavia and Slovenia.
American Revolutionary War: British forces caught up with American troops withdrawing from Ticonderoga, capturing more than 200 men at the Battle of Hubbardton.
US president William McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution, annexing Hawaii as a territory of the United States.
Four countries signed the North Pacific Fur Seal Convention, which banned the hunting of seals in the pelagic zone.

links.title: North Pacific Fur Seal Convention of 1911

facts.text: West Germany won the FIFA World Cup final against the Netherlands at the Munich Olympiastadion.
A U.S. Army Reserve veteran ambushed and shot at police officers in Dallas, killing five of them and injuring nine others, before being killed by a bomb attached to a police robot.

image.caption: Location 32°46′46.4″N 96°48′15.4″W ﻿ / ﻿ 32.779556°N 96.804278°W ﻿ / 32.779556; -96.804278 Main Street and S. Lamar Street, Dallas , Texas, U.S [ 1 ]

facts.text: Baptist minister John Clarke was granted the Rhode Island Royal Charter, described as the "grandest instrument of human liberty ever constructed".
Great Northern War: Swedish forces under Charles XII were defeated by Russian troops led by Peter the Great at the Battle of Poltava.
French and Indian War: French forces defeated the British at Fort Carillon in the British colony of New York.
Korean War: American troops withdrew from Cheonan, in modern-day South Korea, after suffering heavy casualties from a North Korean attack.
Following student protests at Rangoon University, Burmese general Ne Win ordered the demolition of the historic students' union building.
Canadian Pacific Air Lines Flight 21 was destroyed by a bomb near 100 Mile House, Canada, killing 52.
King Mwambutsa IV of Burundi was deposed in a coup d'état by his son, Prince Charles Ndizi.
Aeroflot Flight 4225 crashed near Almaty International Airport in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic (present day Kazakhstan ) killing all 166 people on board.
Sudan Airways Flight 139 crashed near Port Sudan Airport during an emergency landing attempt, killing 116 of the 117 people on board.
German citizen Lars Mittank disappeared from Varna Airport, Bulgaria; his last known movements were widely watched on YouTube.
In the 2014 FIFA World Cup semi-final at the Mineirão, Germany defeated Brazil 7–1, breaking several tournament records.

links.title: Brazil v Germany (2014 FIFA World Cup)

facts.text: Head of a Bear sold at auction in London for a total of £8.8 million, a record for a drawing by Leonardo da Vinci.
The United States Declaration of Independence received its first formal public reading, in Philadelphia.
Members of the North-West Mounted Police at Fort Dufferin began their March West, their first journey to the Canadian Prairies.
Following reports of the capture of a "flying disc" by U.S. Army Air Forces personnel near Roswell, New Mexico, the military stated that the crashed object was a conventional weather balloon.
West Germany won the FIFA World Cup final against defending champions Argentina, with Andreas Brehme scoring the game's only goal.
Former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe was assassinated with an improvised firearm due to resentment against the Unification Church.

image.caption: Location 34°41′38.6″N 135°47′02.2″E ﻿ / ﻿ 34.694056°N 135.783944°E ﻿ / 34.694056; 135.783944 near Yamato-Saidaiji Station in Nara, Nara Prefecture , Japan

facts.text: The Virginia Governor's Council made John Punch the first legally recognized slave in England's North American colonies.
War of the Austrian Succession: French victory at the Battle of Melle enabled their subsequent capture of Ghent from the Austrian Netherlands.
Russo-Swedish War: During the Battle of Svensksund in the Baltic Sea, the Swedish Navy captured a third of the Russian fleet.
British explorer David Thompson posted a notice at the confluence of the Columbia and Snake Rivers (in modern Washington state, U.S.), claiming the area for Great Britain.
Following Zachary Taylor 's death, Millard Fillmore became president of the United States, the last member of the Whig Party to hold that office.
The Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, including the Citizenship Clause and the Equal Protection Clause, was ratified by the minimum required twenty-eight states.

links.title: Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

facts.text: The inaugural Wimbledon Championship, the world's oldest tennis tournament, began in London.
Politician William Jennings Bryan made his Cross of Gold speech advocating bimetallism, considered one of the greatest political speeches in American history.
Nitrate film being stored in a 20th Century Fox facility spontaneously combusted, destroying more than 40,000 reels of negatives and film prints.
World War II: The Battle of Saipan concluded after a mass Japanese suicide attack was repelled by American forces.

Albert Einstein, Bertrand Russell and nine other preeminent intellectuals and scientists issued the Russell–Einstein Manifesto, calling for a conference to assess the dangers posed by weapons of mass destruction.

links.title: Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs

facts.text: An earthquake struck Lituya Bay, Alaska; the subsequent megatsunami, the largest in modern times, reached an elevation of 1,720 ft (524 m).
The United States conducted the Starfish Prime high-altitude nuclear test, the largest nuclear explosion in outer space.
In a seminal moment for pop art, Andy Warhol 's Campbell's Soup Cans exhibition opened at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles.
A British man named Michael Fagan broke into Buckingham Palace and entered Queen Elizabeth II 's bedroom when she was asleep.
Sri Lankan civil war: After advising civilians to take shelter in places of worship, the Sri Lanka Air Force bombed a church in Navaly, killing at least 147 people.
An estimated 30,000 people died when a massive earthquake struck the Roman province of Phoenice.
The Mozart family grand tour began, presenting child prodigies Maria Anna and Wolfgang in Western Europe.
Nintendo released the arcade game Donkey Kong, which featured the debut of Mario, one of the most famous characters in video-game history.
Italy won their fourth World Cup title, defeating France 5–3 on penalties following a 1–1 draw after extra time.
Under the belief that Israel and the United States were planning to attack its nuclear program, Iran conducted the Great Prophet III missile test and war games exercise.
In a plot to eliminate the Japanese Soga clan, Prince Naka no Ōe assassinated Soga no Iruka (depicted), beginning the Isshi incident.
Zhu Chenhao declared Ming emperor Zhengde to be a usurper, beginning the Prince of Ning rebellion.
English Civil War: The Parliamentarians destroyed the last Royalist field army at the Battle of Langport, ultimately giving Parliament control of the west of England.
Anglo-Spanish War (1654–1660): Henry Morgan with an English privateer force landed at Porto Bello (in modern-day Panama) in an attempt to capture the Spanish city.

links.title: Henry Morgan's raid on Porto Bello

facts.text: Indian sepoys mutinied against the East India Company at Vellore Fort.
The air temperature in Furnace Creek, California, reached 134 °F (56.7 °C), recognized by the World Meteorological Organization as the highest recorded on Earth.
Indian mystic and spiritual master Meher Baba began his silence until his death in 1969, only communicating by means of an alphabet board or by unique hand gestures.
A downed Japanese Mitsubishi A6M Zero was discovered on Akutan Island, Alaska; it was later rebuilt and flown to devise tactics against the aircraft during World War II.

Three African-American United States Marines who repeatedly raped local women in Katsuyama near Nago, Okinawa were killed by the residents and had their bodies hidden in a nearby cave for over 50 years.
Martin Luther King Jr. led a rally in support of the Chicago Freedom Movement, one of the most ambitious civil-rights campaigns in the northern United States.
John Paul Getty III, a grandson of the American oil magnate J. Paul Getty, was kidnapped in Rome.
Moktar Ould Daddah, the first president of Mauritania, was ousted in a coup d'état led by Mustafa Ould Salek.

links.title: List of heads of state of Mauritania

facts.text: The United States defeated China in the final match of the third FIFA Women's World Cup, setting records in both attendance and television ratings for women's sports.

links.title: United States women's national soccer team

facts.text: Typhoon Ewiniar made landfall in South Korea, causing damages across the country amounting to 2.06 trillion won (US$1.4 billion).

The last edition of the British tabloid News of the World was published, closing due to allegations that it hacked the voicemails of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler, victims of the 7/7 attacks and relatives of deceased British soldiers.
The last members of a junior association football team and their coach were rescued from Tham Luang Nang Non, a flooded cave in northern Thailand.

The Treaty of Tagilde was signed between Ferdinand I of Portugal and representatives of John of Gaunt of England, marking the beginning of the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance, which remains in effect today.
Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed the successor to King Edward VI of England, beginning her disputed reign as the "Nine Days' Queen".

image.caption: Queen of England and Ireland ( more... ) (disputed)

facts.text: Irish War of Independence: One day after a truce was agreed between the Irish Republican Army and British forces, violence broke out between Catholics and Protestants in Belfast.
The Holocaust: Ethnic Poles murdered at least 340 Jewish residents of Jedwabne in German-occupied Poland.
The Russian river cruise liner Bulgaria was caught in a storm in Tatarstan on the Volga River and sank in several minutes, resulting in 122 deaths.
Byzantine emperor Michael I Rangabe (depicted), under threat by conspiracies, abdicated in favor of his general Leo the Armenian, and became a monk.
Franco-Flemish War: Flemish infantry defeated a large French army near Kortrijk at the Battle of the Golden Spurs.
Marking the start of the Ming treasure voyages, a Chinese expeditionary fleet led by Zheng He set sail for foreign regions of the South China Sea and the Indian Ocean.
French Revolution: Jacques Necker was dismissed as Director-General of Finances of France, sparking public demonstrations in Paris that led to the storming of the Bastille.

links.title: List of Finance Ministers of France

facts.text: The Belfast Harp Festival, an early event in the Gaelic revival, began at the Assembly Rooms.
French astronomer Jean-Louis Pons co-discovered the first of his 37 comets, more than any other person in history.
British soldier Frederick John White died after a flogging, leading to a campaign to end the practice in the British Army.
Waterloo Bridge Station, which later became Britain's busiest railway station by passenger usage, was opened by the London and South Western Railway.

links.title: List of busiest railway stations in Great Britain

facts.text: American Civil War: Confederate forces under Jubal Early began an unsuccessful attempt to capture Washington, D.C..
A riot broke out in Leicester, England, at the failed launching of a gas balloon.
The US Navy launched the USS Nevada (BB-36) as its first Standard-type battleship.
Archaeologist Ivan Borkovský discovered a medieval skeleton at Prague Castle; competing factions claimed the skeleton as Germanic or Slavic in origin.
To Kill a Mockingbird, a novel by Harper Lee featuring themes of racial injustice and the loss of innocence in the Deep South of America, was published.
The Islamist militia group Al-Shabaab carried out multiple suicide bombings in Kampala, Uganda, killing 74 people and injuring 85 others.
An explosion at the Evangelos Florakis Naval Base killed 13 people, including the head of the Cyprus Navy.

Yagan, a Noongar warrior wanted for leading attacks on British colonists in Western Australia, was killed, becoming a symbol of the unjust and sometimes brutal treatment of indigenous Australians by colonial settlers.
New York City's Triborough Bridge, the "biggest traffic machine ever built", opened to traffic.
Italy defeated West Germany 3–1 to win their third FIFA World Cup title.
Shortly after taking off from Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, Nigeria Airways Flight 2120 caught fire and crashed, killing all 261 people on board.
Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time to win their first FIFA World Cup title.

King Æthelstan of England secured the submission of four northern rulers: Constantine II of Scotland, Hywel Dda of Deheubarth, Ealdred I of Bamburgh, and Owain ap Dyfnwal of Strathclyde, leading to seven years of peace.
Choe Bu, an official of the Joseon dynasty, returned to Korea after months of shipwrecked travel in China.
French Revolutionary Wars: A squadron of British ships of the line defeated a larger squadron of Spanish and French vessels in the Strait of Gibraltar.
Up to ten people died in a riot between Catholics and members of the Orange Order in Woodstock, New Brunswick.
Second Balkan War: The Serbian Army began the Siege of Vidin, which they abandoned six days later when an armistice between the Serbs and Bulgarians was signed.
First World War: Second Lieutenant Kléber Dupuy defeated a German attack on Fort Souville at a key moment of the Battle of Verdun.
An explosion in the ammunition magazine of the Japanese battleship Kawachi resulted in the deaths of more than 600 officers and crewmen.
The Soviet–Lithuanian Peace Treaty was signed, with Soviet Russia agreeing to recognize an independent Lithuania.
World War II: German and Soviet forces engaged each other at the Battle of Prokhorovka, one of the largest tank battles in military history.

image.caption: Date 12 July 1943 [ a ] Location Prokhorovka , Russian SFSR , Soviet Union 51°2′11″N 36°44′11″E ﻿ / ﻿ 51.03639°N 36.73639°E ﻿ / 51.03639; 36.73639 Result See § Outcome

facts.text: Arab–Israeli War: Israel Defense Forces officer Yitzhak Rabin signed an order to expel Palestinians from the towns of Lydda and Ramle.

links.title: Palestinian expulsion from Lydda and Ramle

facts.text: The English rock band the Rolling Stones played their first concert at the Marquee Club in London.
Hayao Miyazaki 's animated film Princess Mononoke is released, becoming the highest-grossing film in Japan for a few months.

links.title: List of highest-grossing films in Japan

facts.text: Two U.S. Army AH-64 Apache helicopters conducted a series of air-to-ground attacks in Baghdad.
An edit on the page of the coati nicknamed it the Brazilian aardvark, in which multiple news channels followed in pursuit.
Saint Basil's Cathedral, located in Red Square, Moscow, was consecrated.
Sixteen-year-old Pauline Reade, the first victim of serial killers Ian Brady and Myra Hindley, disappeared in Gorton, England.
Rowdy fans at Comiskey Park in Chicago stormed the field during a Major League Baseball promotional event at which a crate of disco records was blown up.
France defeated the defending champions Brazil 3–0 to win their first FIFA World Cup title.
Hezbollah forces crossed the Israel–Lebanon border and attacked Israeli military positions while firing rockets and mortars at Israeli towns, sparking a five-week war.
Livonian Crusade: Samogitian forces defeated Teutonic knights and the Livonian Order at the Battle of Durbe.
Anglo–Spanish War: A convoy of English ships from the Levant Company repelled a fleet of Spanish and Maltese galleys at the Battle of Pantelleria.
Four days of rioting began in New York City in response to laws passed by the U.S. Congress to draft men to fight in the American Civil War.
While on a campaign in Bulgaria, the Romanian Army suffered a cholera outbreak that led to around 1,600 deaths.
The first FIFA World Cup was opened in Uruguay.
World War II: The 1st Filipino Infantry Regiment was converted from a battalion to accommodate a larger number of volunteers spurred on by the Japanese invasion of the Philippines.
World War II: Operation Fustian, an Allied operation to capture the Primosole Bridge in Sicily, was launched.
Watergate scandal: Under questioning by Senate investigators, White House deputy chief of staff Alexander Butterfield revealed the existence of a secret taping system in the Oval Office.
Croatian War of Independence: The Croatian Army concluded Operation Tiger, advancing 17 kilometres (11 miles) into the Dubrovnik hinterland.
French Directorate General for External Security personnel aborted an operation to rescue Colombian politician Íngrid Betancourt from FARC guerrillas, resulting in a political scandal.
Typhoon Soulik made landfall in East China and Taiwan, killing at least 20 people.
After a five day search, the body of American actress and singer Naya Rivera was recovered from Lake Piru, confirming her death.
English Civil War: Royalist forces defeated the Parliamentarians at the Battle of Roundway Down near Devizes, Wiltshire.
The Battle of Trippstadt between French forces and those of Prussia and Austria began.
Wallachian officials adopted the Regulamentul Organic, which engendered a period of reforms that provided for the westernization of the local society.
In an unprecedented reshuffle, British prime minister Harold Macmillan dismissed seven members of his cabinet.
Germany won the FIFA World Cup final against Argentina, with Mario Götze scoring the game's only goal in the extra time.
The Bastille, a fortress and prison in Paris, was stormed by a crowd during the flashpoint of the French Revolution.
The Priestley Riots, targeting religious dissenters such as Joseph Priestley, began in Birmingham, England.
A fire destroyed 812 structures and killed 20 people in Chicago, leading to reforms in the city's fire-prevention and firefighting efforts.
While on the run from a death sentence, American outlaw Billy the Kid was shot and killed by Sherriff Pat Garrett in Fort Sumner, New Mexico.
The medieval St Mark's Campanile in Venice collapsed, also demolishing the Loggetta del Sansovino.
An expedition led by Peruvian explorer and farmer Agustín Lizárraga discovered the Incan city of Machu Picchu.

image.caption: Born Agustín Lizárraga Ruiz ( 1865-06-12 ) 12 June 1865 Mollepata, Cusco , Peru

facts.text: The Battle of Delville Wood began as an action within the Battle of the Somme, lasting until 3 September 1916.
Korean War: North Korean troops began attacking the headquarters of the American 24th Infantry Division in present-day Daejeon, South Korea.
More than 100 mm (3.9 in) of rain fell in a two-and-a-half-hour period in parts of Montreal, causing severe flooding.
Valerie Plame 's identity as a CIA operative was leaked to and published by journalist Robert Novak.
A man deliberately drove a truck into crowds in Nice, France, resulting in 86 deaths.
Louis VIII became King of France and began a three-year reign.
The Sedition Act became law, making it a federal crime to write, publish, or utter false or malicious statements about the U.S. government.

links.title: Federal government of the United States

facts.text: A seven-man team made the first ascent of the Matterhorn, marking the end of the golden age of alpinism.
Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 1-11 ditched off Polillo Island in the Philippines, killing one person and injuring 44.
Lightning strikes started four fires in the Methow River in the American state of Washington, collectively known as the Carlton Complex Fire.
French soldiers at Fort Julien, near the Egyptian port city of Rashid, uncovered the Rosetta Stone, which was essential in the decipherment of ancient Egyptian scripts.
Following the transfer of Rupert's Land from the Hudson's Bay Company, Manitoba was established as a province of Canada.
The all-female Emilia Plater Independent Women's Battalion was formed in the Soviet Union's First Polish Army.
Caspian Airlines Flight 7908 crashed in northwestern Iran, killing all 168 people aboard.
South Korean rapper Psy released his hit single " Gangnam Style ".
The Peace at Home Council, a faction of the Turkish Armed Forces, staged a coup d'état attempt against the government and President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald, the decisive engagement of the Polish–Lithuanian–Teutonic War.

links.title: Crown of the Kingdom of Poland

facts.text: Aboard HMS Bellerophon, French emperor Napoleon surrendered to Royal Navy captain Frederick Lewis Maitland, concluding the Napoleonic Wars.
Sega 's first home video game console, the SG-1000, was released in Japan.
A M w 7.8 earthquake struck a remote region of Fiordland, New Zealand, the country's largest earthquake magnitude since the 1931 Hawke's Bay earthquake.
Croatian Mario Mandžukić scored the first own goal in a FIFA World Cup final in their defeat to France.
The ten-year-old Richard II was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart 's opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail premiered in Vienna, after which Emperor Joseph II anecdotally remarked that it had "too many notes".
President George Washington signed the Residence Act, selecting a new permanent site along the Potomac River for the capital of the United States, which later became Washington, D.C.
Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie promulgated the nation's first modern constitution.
The United States conducted the first detonation of a nuclear weapon during the Trinity test.
Korean War: A Korean People's Army unit massacred 31 prisoners of war of the U.S. Army on a mountain near the village of Tuman.

South Vietnamese Colonel Phạm Ngọc Thảo —an undetected communist spy —was reported dead due to injuries sustained during his capture, but it is generally assumed he was killed on the orders of military officials.

image.caption: Born ( 1922-02-14 ) 14 February 1922 Can Tho , Cochinchina, French Indochina

links.title: Army of the Republic of Vietnam

facts.text: A Sikorsky S-61 helicopter operated by British Airways crashed in thick fog in the Celtic Sea, killing 20 of the 26 people on board.

links.title: 1983 British Airways Helicopters Sikorsky S-61 crash

facts.text: A 7.8 M S earthquake struck the densely populated Philippine island of Luzon, killing an estimated 1,621 people.
Fragments of Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 began colliding with the planet Jupiter, with the first impact causing a fireball that reached a peak temperature of 24,000 kelvin.
Millennium Park, a public park in Chicago, Illinois, and one of the world's largest rooftop gardens, opened to the public.
A tainted milk powder scandal broke in China which ultimately involved an estimated 300,000 victims, the vast majority infants, with 54,000 hospitalized with kidney problems and six deaths.
At least 23 students died and dozens more fell ill at a primary school in the Indian state of Bihar after consuming a Midday Meal that was contaminated with pesticide.
Muhammad ibn Yusuf, who later established the Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state in Spain, was elected the ruler of Arjona.
Uruguay won the decisive match of the FIFA World Cup against Brazil 2–1 at Maracanã Stadium, Rio de Janeiro.

links.title: Uruguay v Brazil (1950 FIFA World Cup)

facts.text: Max Reger 's Hebbel Requiem was first performed in a memorial concert for the composer, conducted by Philipp Wolfrum.
The Catcher in the Rye, an American coming-of-age novel by J. D. Salinger, was first published.
An earthquake of magnitude M w 6.6 struck Niigata Prefecture, Japan, causing a leak of radioactive gases from the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Plant.
The Battle of Castillon, the last engagement of the Hundred Years' War, ended with the English losing all holdings in France except the Pale of Calais.
William Cranch Bond and John Adams Whipple took a daguerreotype of Vega, the first astrophotograph of a star other than the Sun.
The garrotting and robbery of James Pilkington, a British member of Parliament, led to a moral panic in London.
RMS Carpathia, which had rescued survivors of the 1912 Titanic sinking, was sunk by a German U-boat with the loss of five crew.
Russian Revolution: Tsar Nicholas II and his family were murdered by Bolsheviks at Yekaterinburg.
Laden with munitions for World War II, two ships exploded at the Port Chicago Naval Magazine in California, killing 320 people and injuring more than 400 others.

links.title: Port Chicago Naval Magazine National Memorial

facts.text: In Olympia, Greece, the Summer Olympics torch relay, nicknamed the "relay of peace", began.
The Manchester Metrolink, the first modern street-running light-rail system in the United Kingdom, was officially opened.
TWA Flight 800 exploded in mid-air and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York.
Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was shot down over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 people on board.
Dene men, acting as guides to Samuel Hearne on his exploration of the Coppermine River in present-day Nunavut, Canada, massacred a group of about twenty Copper Inuit.
The New Zealand Wars resumed as British forces led by General Duncan Cameron began the invasion of the Waikato.
Led by Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party overthrew Iraqi president Abdul Rahman Arif in a bloodless coup.
Brazil won the FIFA World Cup final against Italy 3–2 on penalties following a 0–0 draw after extra time.
TAM Airlines Flight 3054 overran the runway at Congonhas Airport in São Paulo, Brazil, killing 199 people.
An explosion at a gunpowder magazine in Birgu, Malta, killed an estimated 200 people.
Pedro II, the last emperor of Brazil, was crowned at the Old Cathedral of Rio de Janeiro.

links.title: Coronation of the Emperor of Brazil
Old Cathedral of Rio de Janeiro

facts.text: American Civil War: Led by Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment, one of the first African-American military units in the Union Army, spearheaded an assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina.
Newsboys from Long Island City turned over a distribution wagon for the New York Journal, marking the start of the Newsboys' strike of 1899.
Nationalist rebels attempted a coup against the Second Spanish Republic, sparking the Spanish Civil War.
Francisco Javier Arana, the chief of the Guatemalan armed forces, was killed in a shootout with supporters of President Juan José Arévalo.
Angered by racism and poverty, African American residents of the Hough neighborhood of Cleveland began to riot for six days.
Parts of the dismembered body of Swedish prostitute Catrine da Costa were found in Stockholm.
A gunman massacred 21 people and injured 15 others at a McDonald's restaurant in the district of San Ysidro of San Diego, California.
A suicide bomber attacked an Israeli tour bus at Burgas Airport, Bulgaria, resulting in the military branch of Hezbollah being designated a terrorist organization by the European Union.
The conviction of former Italian prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who had been found guilty of paying for an underage prostitute, was overturned on appeal.
An arson attack at the studio of Kyoto Animation in Japan led to the deaths of 36 people.
King Edward I issued an edict to expel all Jews from England.

links.title: History of the Jews in England

facts.text: Johann Sebastian Bach directed the first performance of his cantata Erforsche mich, Gott, und erfahre mein Herz in Leipzig.

links.title: Erforsche mich, Gott, und erfahre mein Herz, BWV 136

facts.text: At the Olympic Games in Montreal, Nadia Comăneci became the first person to score a perfect 10 in a modern Olympics gymnastics event.
American actress Rebecca Schaeffer was shot and killed by Robert John Bardo, eventually prompting the passage of anti- stalking laws in California.
Selena 's album Dreaming of You, instrumental in popularizing Tejano music, was released posthumously.
Arab–Byzantine wars: After initial Byzantine gains at the Battle of Apamea, a lone Kurdish rider killed Byzantine commander Damian Dalassenos, allowing Fatimid troops to turn the tide of the battle.
Second War of Scottish Independence: Scottish forces under Sir Archibald Douglas were heavily defeated by the English at the Battle of Halidon Hill while trying to relieve Berwick-upon-Tweed.
The English warship Mary Rose sank outside Portsmouth during the Battle of the Solent; it was raised from the seabed in 1982.
Mary I was proclaimed Queen of England, deposing Lady Jane Grey after nine days of de facto rule.
Great Northern War: Polish – Saxon forces were defeated by a Swedish army half their size at the Battle of Kliszów.
Georg Anton Schäffer was forced to depart for China after his unsuccessful attempt to seize the Hawaiian Kingdom for the Russian Empire.
SS Great Britain, the first ocean-going ship with both an iron hull and a screw propeller, was launched in Bristol, England.
The two-day Seneca Falls Convention, the first women's-rights and feminist convention held in the United States, opened in Seneca Falls, New York.
First World War: The "worst 24 hours in Australia's entire history" occurred when Australian forces unsuccessfully attacked German defences at Fromelles, France.
The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold, a largely autobiographical novel by Evelyn Waugh, was published.
Environmental activists bombed the port facilities in Bunbury, Western Australia, in an attempt to disrupt the woodchipping industry.
A car bomb killed the anti- Mafia judge Paolo Borsellino and five policemen in Palermo, Italy, less than two months after the murder of Borsellino's friend and colleague Giovanni Falcone.
Gunmen ambushed an Egyptian military checkpoint in the Libyan Desert near Farafra, killing 22 soldiers.
Neary's, a New York City Irish pub popular with political elites, closed.
A fire in Manhattan, New York, destroyed 345 buildings, killed 30 people, and caused at least $5 million in damage.

links.title: Great New York City Fire of 1845

facts.text: French cyclist Maurice Garin won the first edition of the Tour de France.
Following Peace Day celebrations marking the end of the First World War, English ex-servicemen unhappy with unemployment and other grievances rioted and burned down Luton Town Hall.
The Troubles: The Provisional Irish Republican Army announced that it would resume its ceasefire, ending its 28-year campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland.
The NASA spacecraft Cassini took a photograph of Saturn with Earth in the distance, for which people were invited to "wave at Saturn".
Second War of Scottish Inde­pen­dence: The Scottish-held town of Berwick-upon-Tweed surrendered to English forces, ending a siege led by King Edward III.
Wars of the Three Kingdoms: After crossing the Firth of Forth, English Commonwealth forces defeated a Scottish army at the Battle of Inverkeithing, opening the rest of the country to occupation.
Scottish explorer Alexander Mackenzie reached the Pacific coast at Bella Coola, British Columbia, completing the first recorded transcontinental crossing of North America north of Mexico.
The United States Congress established the Indian Peace Commission to seek peace treaties with a number of Native American tribes.

links.title: Native Americans in the United States

facts.text: George V reviewed more than 200 Royal Navy vessels at Spithead, England.
Serbian prime minister Nikola Pašić and Yugoslav Committee president Ante Trumbić signed the Corfu Declaration, agreeing to seek the establishment of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.
Korean War: After a month-long campaign, much of the North Korean air force was destroyed by United Nations forces.

links.title: Korean People's Army Air and Anti-Air Force

facts.text: The first games of the Special Olympics, for athletes with intellectual disabilities, were held at Soldier Field in Chicago.
The Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle landed on the Sea of Tranquillity, where Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first men to walk on the Moon six and a half hours later.
Rain from a stalled thunderstorm caused six dams to fail, flooding Johnstown, Pennsylvania, resulting in 84 deaths and $340 in damages.
Members of the Provisional Irish Republican Army detonated two bombs in Hyde Park and Regent's Park in London, killing eleven British Army personnel and seven horses.

links.title: Hyde Park and Regent's Park bombings

facts.text: Twenty-three-year-old Italian anti-globalist Carlo Giuliani was shot dead by a police officer while protesting outside the 27th G8 summit held in Genoa, Italy.
A gunman carried out a mass shooting at a movie theater in Aurora, Colorado, killing 12 people and injuring 58 others.
French brothers Claude and Nicéphore Niépce received a patent for their Pyréolophore, one of the world's first internal combustion engines.
Abdullah I of Jordan was assassinated while visiting the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.

links.title: Assassination of Abdullah I of Jordan

facts.text: The Viking 1 lander became the first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars and perform its mission.
USS Constitution, one of the United States Navy 's original six frigates, sailed for the first time in 116 years after a full restoration.

links.title: Original six frigates of the United States Navy

facts.text: A suicide attack in Suruç, Turkey, for which Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) claimed responsibility, killed 34 people and injured 104 others.
Pope Pontian began his pontificate, succeeding Urban I.
A large earthquake occurred near Crete, triggering a tsunami, and causing widespread destruction around the eastern Mediterranean region.
Paulinus was consecrated as the first bishop of York by Justus, the archbishop of Canterbury.
Unrepresented labourers revolted and violently took over the government of the Republic of Florence (depicted), demanding that they be granted political office.
World War I: An Imperial German Navy U-boat opened fire on a small convoy of barges and defending aircraft near the American town of Orleans, Massachusetts.
American high school biology teacher John T. Scopes was found guilty of violating Tennessee 's Butler Act by teaching evolution in class.
After weeks of unrest, rioters lynched Bolivian president Gualberto Villarroel, desecrating and hanging his corpse in the streets of La Paz.
An earthquake registering 7.3 M w struck the southern San Joaquin Valley in California, causing 12 deaths and an estimated $60 million in property damage.
The inaugural International Mathematical Olympiad, the leading mathematical competition for pre-university students, began in Romania.
The Troubles: The Provisional Irish Republican Army detonated twenty-two bombs throughout Belfast, Northern Ireland.
Libyan forces carried out a raid at Sallum, sparking a four-day war with Egypt.
Nour Ahmad Nikbakht, an Iranian diplomat in Yemen, was kidnapped by al-Qaeda militants and held hostage for the next two years.
People returning from anti-extradition bill protests were attacked by suspected triad members in Yuen Long, Hong Kong, leaving 45 people injured.
Louis III, Holy Roman Emperor, was captured and blinded during his attempt to restore Carolingian power over Italy by King Berengar I.
Much of central Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, was burned and looted during the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
Sirimavo Bandaranaike was sworn in as prime minister of Ceylon, becoming the world's first democratically elected female head of government.

links.title: List of elected and appointed female heads of state and government

facts.text: The Taiwanese military ordered the deportation of dozens of illegal immigrants from mainland China in sealed boat holds, causing 25 deaths due to suffocation.

Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, the final book in the popular Harry Potter series by J. K. Rowling, was released and sold 15 million copies in its first 24 hours, making it the fastest-selling book in history.

links.title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows

facts.text: Arab–Byzantine wars: The forces of the Abbasid Caliphate defeated Byzantine troops led by Emperor Theophilos at the Battle of Anzen, near present-day Dazman, Turkey.
First War of Scottish Independence: English forces led by Edward I defeated William Wallace 's Scottish troops at the Battle of Falkirk.
Gia Long conquered Hanoi and unified modern-day Vietnam, which had experienced centuries of feudal warfare.
Windham William Sadler made the first successful aerial crossing of the Irish Sea, which he accomplished by balloon.
American Civil War: Confederate forces unsuccessfully attacked Union troops at the Battle of Atlanta.
Jules-Albert de Dion finished first in the world's first motor race, but did not win as his steam-powered car was against the rules.
World War II: In opposition to the government-in-exile based in London, the Soviet-backed Polish Committee of National Liberation was proclaimed to govern territory recaptured from Germany.

links.title: Manifesto of the Polish Committee of National Liberation

facts.text: A limited state of martial law was declared in Russell County, Alabama, due to organized crime.

links.title: Declaration of martial law in Russell County, Alabama

facts.text: Stanley Forman took the Pulitzer Prize –winning photo Fire Escape Collapse, which spurred action to improve the safety of fire escapes across the United States.

image.caption: Born Stanley Joseph Forman ( 1945-07-10 ) July 10, 1945 (age 80) Winthrop, Massachusetts , U.S.

facts.text: American serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer was arrested in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, after police discovered human remains in his apartment.
Written and illustrated by Eiichiro Oda, One Piece, the best-selling manga series in history, debuted in Weekly Shōnen Jump.
The Israel Defense Forces bombed the home of Salah Shehade, the leader of the military arm of Hamas, killing him, his family and neighboring civilians.
A crusader army captured Béziers, France, and massacred the city's inhabitants in the first major military action of the Albigensian Crusade.
Williamite forces defeated the Jacobites at the Battle of Aughrim, the decisive battle of the Williamite War in Ireland.
Soviet space dogs: Dezik and Tsygan were launched into a sub-orbital spaceflight from Kapustin Yar and became the first dogs to fly in space and the first to safely return.
The United Kingdom granted self-government to Sarawak, the day would be celebrated as Sarawak Day.

image.caption: Nickname(s) : Bumi Kenyalang [ 1 ] (English: "Land of the Hornbills " )

facts.text: Japan completed its last reparation to the Philippines for war crimes committed during imperial Japan's conquest of the country in the Second World War.
A fleet led by the Knights Hospitaller sank 22 of 28 ships of the Turkish Aydinid emirate.
The trial of the Eastbourne manslaughter, which later became an important legal precedent in the United Kingdom for discussions of corporal punishment in schools, began in Lewes.
During a visit of the French Navy to Kronstadt in Russia, the two nations reached a secret agreement on a joint response to any future war in Europe.
Wilfred Rhodes of England and Yorkshire became the only person to play in 1,000 first-class cricket matches.
The Holocaust: The gas chambers at Treblinka extermination camp began operation, killing 6,500 Jews who had been transported from the Warsaw Ghetto the day before.
A shootout between police and a Black power group began in Cleveland, Ohio, sparking three days of rioting.
Vanessa Williams, the first African-American Miss America, was forced to resign after the magazine Penthouse published nude photos of her without consent.
Hale–Bopp, one of the most widely observed comets of the 20th century, was independently discovered by astronomers Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp.
In Tulia, Texas, 47 people were arrested for dealing cocaine; years later, 35 of the 47 were pardoned by the Governor of Texas.
The first National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party opened in a house in Shanghai.

links.title: 1st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party
Site of the First National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party

facts.text: Sumner Welles, U.S. Under Secretary of State, issued a declaration that the U.S. government would not recognize the Soviet Union's annexation of the Baltic states.

links.title: United States Under Secretary of State

facts.text: A helicopter crashed during the filming of Twilight Zone: The Movie in Valencia, California, killing actor Vic Morrow and two child actors.
Megawati Sukarnoputri was sworn in as the first female president of Indonesia following her predecessor's impeachment.
The English-Irish boy band One Direction were formed while auditioning for the 2010 series of the British singing competition The X Factor.

links.title: The X Factor (British TV series) series 7

facts.text: The Ostrogoths abandoned the Siege of Ariminum upon the arrival of the Byzantine fleet.
Mary, Queen of Scots, was forced to abdicate in favour of her one-year-old son, who became James VI.
During a speech in Montreal, French president Charles de Gaulle declared " Long live free Quebec! ", a statement that was interpreted as support for Quebec independence from Canada.
Australia set a world record for the highest successful run-chase in Test cricket history during the Fourth Test of the Ashes series against England.
Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev and U.S. vice president Richard Nixon held an impromptu debate at the opening of the American National Exhibition at Sokolniki Park in Moscow.
The Metapolitefsi period began with Konstantinos Karamanlis taking office as Prime Minister of Greece after the collapse of the military junta.

The Australian swimming team, nicknamed the Quietly Confident Quartet, won the men's 4 × 100 metre medley relay at the Moscow Olympics, the only time that the United States, which boycotted the games, has not won the event at the Olympics.

links.title: Swimming at the 1980 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 × 100 metre medley relay

facts.text: Iran–Iraq War: In opposition to the American plan to protect Kuwaiti tankers, Iran laid mines and damaged the SS Bridgeton, resulting in a propaganda victory for Iran.
A gunman entered the United States Capitol and opened fire, killing two police officers.
Air Algérie Flight 5017 disappeared from radar shortly after take-off from Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso; its wreckage was found the following day in Mali with no survivors.
Scottish clansmen led by Donald of Islay, Lord of the Isles, and Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar, fought the Battle of Harlaw near Inverurie, Scotland.

links.title: Donald of Islay, Lord of the Isles

facts.text: Ottoman forces captured the city of Shkodër, ending the Albanian revolt of 1910 (depicted).
Franco-Syrian War: At the Battle of Maysalun forces of the Arab Kingdom of Syria were defeated by a French army moving to occupy the territory allocated to them by the San Remo conference.
The Treaty of Lausanne was signed to settle part of the partition of the Ottoman Empire, establishing the boundaries of Greece, Bulgaria and Turkey.
Boris Johnson became Prime Minister of the United Kingdom after winning the Conservative Party leadership election.

links.title: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

facts.text: Constantine the Great was proclaimed Roman emperor by his troops after the death of Constantius Chlorus.
Henry II was crowned King of France at Reims Cathedral.
Eighty Years' War: Dutch and English forces relieved the siege of Knodsenburg in the Spanish Netherlands, having defeated the Duke of Parma 's army in the field.
Mozart completed his Symphony No. 40, one of his two extant symphonies in a minor key.
Spanish–American War: After more than two months of sea-based bombardment, the United States invaded Puerto Rico.
The Grand Council of Fascism voted a motion of no confidence against Benito Mussolini, who was arrested the same day by King Victor Emmanuel III and replaced by Pietro Badoglio.

links.title: Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy

facts.text: The orbiting spacecraft Viking 1 took a photograph of an apparent face on Mars in a classic example of pareidolia.
Phoolan Devi, a serving Member of Parliament, was assassinated by shooting in New Delhi, India.
Pratibha Patil was sworn in as the first female president of India.
Alexios Strategopoulos led Nicaean forces to recapture Constantinople, leading to the reestablishment of the Byzantine Empire and the end of the Latin Empire.

links.title: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty

facts.text: The Corinth Canal was formally opened, bisecting the narrow Isthmus of Corinth in Greece to connect the Ionian Sea 's Gulf of Corinth with the Aegean Sea 's Saronic Gulf.
Korean War: After American troops withdrew, North Korean forces captured the village of Yongdong in South Korea.
Air France Flight 4590, a Concorde en route from Paris to New York, crashed in Gonesse, France, killing all 109 passengers on board and four people on the ground.
WikiLeaks published 75,000 classified documents about the War in Afghanistan in one of the largest leaks in U.S. military history.

links.title: United States documents leak of the War in Afghanistan
Classified information in the United States

facts.text: The Knights Hospitaller surrendered the Castello of Gozo to the Ottoman Empire following a brief siege, leading to the mass enslavement and dispersal of the Gozitan population.
On the orders of Catherine the Great the first of tens of thousands of Greek and Armenian Christians were removed from Crimea and resettled in Pryazovia.

links.title: Eviction of Christians from the Crimea (1778)

facts.text: In Short Creek, Arizona, police conducted a mass arrest of approximately 400 Mormon fundamentalists for polygamy.
Asiana Airlines Flight 733 crashed into a mountain during a failed attempt to land at Mokpo Airport, South Korea, leading to the deaths of 68 people on board.
Hillary Clinton became the first female nominee for president of the United States by a major political party at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia.
L. L. Zamenhof published Unua Libro, the first publication to describe Esperanto, a constructed international language.

image.caption: Born Leyzer Zamengov [ a ] ( 1859-12-15 ) 15 December 1859 [ b ] Belostok , Russian Empire

facts.text: The Canadian National Vimy Memorial, dedicated to Canadian Expeditionary Force members killed in the First World War, was unveiled in Pas-de-Calais, France.
After widespread controversy throughout Wales, Shambo, a black Friesian bull that had been adopted by the local Hindu community, was slaughtered due to concerns about bovine tuberculosis.

French and Indian War: Troops led by French brigadier general François-Charles de Bourlamaque attempted to blow up Fort Carillon, near present-day Ticonderoga, New York, rather than defending it against approaching British forces.
Boer mercenaries established the Republic of Stellaland in land claimed by the United Kingdom as part of British Bechuanaland.

image.caption: Motto: Gewapend en Regtvaardig Dutch : Armed and just(ified)

facts.text: The Battle of the Samichon River, the last engagement of the Korean War, ended a few hours before the signing of the Korean Armistice Agreement.
After coming second to Nguyễn Văn Thiệu in a rigged presidential election, Trương Đình Dzu was jailed by a South Vietnamese military court for illicit currency transactions.
The New Irish Republican Army was formed from a merger of a number of dissident republican militant groups.
Unable to penetrate the city's defences, the Sclaveni gave up their siege of the Byzantine city of Thessalonica.
During his invasion of Scotland, Siward, Earl of Northumbria, defeated Macbeth, King of Scotland, in an engagement north of the Firth of Forth.
Philip II of France decisively won the Battle of Bouvines, the conclusive battle of the 1213–1214 Anglo-French War.
Saint Mary's Church on Gotland, later to become Visby Cathedral, was consecrated.
Byzantine–Ottoman wars: The Ottoman sultanate gained its first major victory against the Byzantine Empire at the Battle of Bapheus in Bithynia.
The Battle of Ushant, the first encounter between the French and British fleets in the American Revolutionary War, ended indecisively and led to political disputes in both countries.
First World War: British mariner Charles Fryatt was executed in Bruges, Belgium, after a German court-martial found him guilty of being a franc-tireur.
Red Summer: Race riots erupted in Chicago after a racial incident occurred on a South Side beach, leading to 38 fatalities and 537 injuries.
Second World War: Allied forces halted the Axis invasion of Egypt at the First Battle of El Alamein.
As the Surprise Hurricane struck Texas, a United States Army Air Forces pilot made the first reconnaissance flight into a hurricane.
The world's first commercial jet airliner to reach production, the de Havilland Comet, had its maiden flight.
An armistice was signed to end hostilities in the Korean War, officially making the division of Korea indefinite by creating a 4 km wide (2.5 mi) demilitarized zone across the Korean Peninsula.
After straying into Bulgarian airspace, El Al Flight 402 was shot down by two MiG-15 fighter jets, resulting in the deaths of all 58 on board.
American musician Madonna released her self-titled debut album, which set the standard for the genre of dance-pop for decades.

Jamaat al Muslimeen, a radical Islamic group, began a coup attempt against the government of Trinidad and Tobago by taking hostages, including Prime Minister A. N. R. Robinson, before surrendering five days later.
Police in Tokyo found the mummified remains of Sogen Kato, thought to have died in 1978, leading to widespread inquiries into the status of isolated elderly people in Japan.
The last nine Aston Martin DB9 units rolled off the production line, marking the end of a twelve-year manufacturing period.
First Jacobite rising: Scottish and Irish Jacobites defeated Williamite forces at Killiecrankie, Scotland.
The Austrian State Treaty came into effect, ending the Allied occupation of Austria, although the country was not free of Allied troops until October.
Mattachine Midwest, a gay rights organization in Chicago, held its first meeting.
While covering a police pursuit in Phoenix, Arizona, two news helicopters collided in mid-air, killing both crews.
A major oil spill from the Colonial Pipeline was discovered in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina.

image.caption: Location Mecklenburg County, North Carolina , United States

facts.text: Crusades: The siege of Damascus ended in a decisive victory for the Muslims, leading to the disintegration of the Second Crusade.
King Henry VIII of England had his chief minister Thomas Cromwell executed for treason and heresy.
Peruvian War of Independence: Argentine general José de San Martín declared the independence of Peru from the Spanish Empire.
Aged 18, Vinnie Ream became the youngest artist and first woman to receive a United States government commission for a statue—that of Abraham Lincoln currently in the Capitol rotunda.
The Australasian Antarctic Expedition began with the departure of SY Aurora from London.
In New York City, the NAACP and church and community leaders organized a silent march of at least 8,000 people to protest violence directed towards African Americans.
During the excavation of a 7th-century ship burial at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk, England, archaeologists discovered a helmet that is widely associated with King Rædwald of East Anglia.
A B-25 bomber crashed into the Empire State Building in New York City, killing 14 people and causing an estimated $1 million in damage.
An earthquake registering 7.6 M w, one of the deadliest in history, devastated Tangshan, China, and killed at least 240,000 people.
Two followers of the Indian mystic Rajneesh were convicted of a 1985 plot to assassinate Charles Turner, the U.S. attorney for the District of Oregon.

links.title: United States District Court for the District of Oregon

facts.text: At the World Aquatics Championships in Fukuoka, Japan, Australian Ian Thorpe became the first swimmer to win six gold medals at a single FINA world championship.
The Provisional Irish Republican Army announced the formal end of its armed campaign to overthrow British rule in Northern Ireland and create a united Ireland.
A Category 1 hurricane made landfall in Azua Province, Dominican Republic, and destroyed three large schooners at Santo Domingo; only one crew member on the three vessels survived.
U.S. Marines landed at Port-au-Prince to begin a nineteen-year occupation of Haiti.
At the Salzburg Conference, Adolf Hitler demanded the replacement of much of Slovakia's cabinet.
Britain's costliest tornado struck Birmingham, injuring 39 people and causing £40 million of damage across the city.
In the deadliest air accident in Pakistan's history, Airblue Flight 202 crashed into the Margalla Hills north of Islamabad, killing all 152 aboard.

links.title: List of deadliest aircraft accidents and incidents

facts.text: Byzantine–Bulgarian wars: Byzantine forces defeated troops of the Bulgarian Empire at the Battle of Kleidion in the mountains of Belasica near present-day Klyuch.
Nine Years' War: French troops defeated the forces of the Grand Alliance led by William III of England at the Battle of Landen in present-day Neerwinden, Belgium.
French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel submitted a memoir on the diffraction of light to the Royal Academy of Sciences, providing strong support for the wave theory of light.
Italian-American anarchist Gaetano Bresci assassinated King Umberto I of Italy in Monza.
The Cape Cod Canal, connecting Cape Cod Bay and Buzzards Bay in the U.S. state of Massachusetts, opened on a limited basis.

image.caption: Location of the Cape Cod Canal

facts.text: The first shots of World War I were fired by the Austro-Hungarian river monitor Bodrog on Serbian defences near Belgrade.
Adolf Hitler became leader of the National Socialist German Workers' Party.
The Essential Commodities Reserves Act, which allowed the British government to build up reserves of essential commodities in anticipation of war, received royal assent.
The Fellowship of the Ring, the first part of J. R. R. Tolkien 's novel The Lord of the Rings, was published by Allen & Unwin.
Arab–Byzantine wars: Thessalonica, the Byzantine Empire 's second-largest city, was sacked by Saracen raiders.
The infant James VI was crowned King of Scotland at Stirling.
In a case later termed a "legal lynching", Will P. Brady obtained a guilty verdict and death sentence against 15-year-old León Martínez Jr., five days after his arrest for killing a white woman.

Korean War: Over fears that North Korean soldiers were infiltrating refugee columns, U.S. forces concluded a four-day massacre of hundreds of civilians through shootings and air attacks near the village of Nogeun-ri.
An estimated worldwide television audience of 750 million watched the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul's Cathedral in London.

links.title: Wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer

facts.text: Bach 's chorale cantata Wo Gott der Herr nicht bei uns hält, a paraphrase of Psalm 124 based on a 1524 hymn by Justus Jonas, was first performed in Leipzig.

links.title: Wo Gott der Herr nicht bei uns hält, BWV 178
Wo Gott der Herr nicht bei uns hält

facts.text: Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla (depicted), a leader of the Mexican War of Independence, was executed by Spanish forces in Chihuahua City, Mexico.
Off the coast of Crescent City, California, the steamer Brother Jonathan struck an uncharted rock and sank, killing 225 people; its cargo of gold coins was not retrieved until 1996.
The boiler of the Staten Island Ferry Westfield II exploded at South Ferry in New York City, killing at least 45 people.
In Montevideo, the Uruguay national football team won the inaugural FIFA World Cup, defeating Argentina 4–2 in the final.
At the height of a political crisis known as the royal question, four workers were shot dead by the Belgian Gendarmerie at a strike in Grâce-Berleur.
American labor-union leader Jimmy Hoffa disappeared after last being seen outside a restaurant near Detroit.
British Conservative member of Parliament Ian Gow was killed outside his home in a car bombing by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.
Lebanon War: The Israeli Air Force attacked a three-story building near the Lebanese village of Qana, killing at least 28 civilians, including 16 children.
More than 150 people died after heavy rains triggered a landslide in the village of Malin in Maharashtra, India.
World War I: German agents sabotaged U.S.-made munitions in New York Harbor that were to be supplied to the Allies.
In London, the England national football team won the FIFA World Cup, winning the final against West Germany 4–2 after extra time.
Amid a widespread economic crisis and food shortages in Poland, up to 50,000 people, mostly women and children, took part in the largest of nationwide hunger demonstrations in Łódź.
A train fire killed 32 passengers and injured 27 on the Tamil Nadu Express in Andhra Pradesh, India.
Emmerson Mnangagwa was elected to his first full term as president, having served as leader since the 2017 Zimbabwean coup d'état.
The Second Anglo-Dutch War ended with the signing of the Treaty of Breda.
Patrick Francis Healy was inaugurated as president of Georgetown University, becoming the first African-American president of a predominantly white university in the United States.
First World War: The Battle of Passchendaele began near Ypres, Belgium, with the Allies aiming to force German troops to withdraw from the Channel Ports.
A private senator's bill by Herbert Payne to introduce compulsory voting in Australia became law.
A team of Italian climbers became the first to reach the summit of K2, the world's second-highest mountain.

links.title: List of highest mountains on Earth

facts.text: The space probe Ranger 7 captured thousands of close-up photographs of the Moon over its final minutes of flight and transmitted them to Earth before crashing on the lunar surface.
The pleasure cruiser MV Darlwyne disappeared off the coast of Cornwall with the loss of all 31 people aboard.

The Troubles: Hours after the British Army 's Operation Motorman brought an end to the self-declared autonomous area of Free Derry in Northern Ireland, three car bombs exploded in the village of Claudy.

image.caption: Outcome British victory Operation against the IRA succeeds.

facts.text: Soviet Special Purpose Police Unit troops killed seven Lithuanian customs officials in Medininkai in the most serious attack of their campaign against Lithuanian border posts.

links.title: Soviet OMON assaults on Lithuanian border posts

facts.text: Three years after being hit by a mudslide, the Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery in Hong Kong fully reopened.
Following intestinal surgery, Fidel Castro provisionally transferred the duties of the Cuban presidency to his brother Raúl.
The Troubles: Operation Banner, the British Armed Forces ' operation in Northern Ireland, ended after 38 years with a military stalemate and ceasefire.
The largest power outage in history occurred across 22 Indian states, affecting more than 620 million people, or about 9 percent of the world's population.

links.title: States and union territories of India

facts.text: Sergius IV became the 142nd pope, succeeding John XVIII.
The Second Continental Congress passed a resolution commissioning the Marquis de Lafayette as a major general in the American revolutionary forces.

image.caption: Nickname The Hero of the Two Worlds ( Le Héros des Deux Mondes ) [ 1 ]

links.title: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette

facts.text: The Holocaust: Under instructions from Adolf Hitler, Hermann Göring authorised SS officer Reinhard Heydrich to handle preparations for "the Final Solution of the Jewish question ".
The Troubles: In a botched paramilitary attack, three members of the popular Miami Showband and two Ulster Volunteer Force gunmen were killed in County Down, Northern Ireland.
Hamas detonated a bomb at the Mount Scopus campus of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, killing nine students and injuring about 100 more.
